assessment.nobel_worthiness: The jamming picture gives a unifying, statistical-mechanical account of how disordered, athermal matter (foams, emulsions, grains, glasses) acquires rigidity at a well-defined critical point with scaling, isostaticity and anomalous vibrational modes. It is conceptually clean, original and has reshaped soft matter and the physics of disordered systems, including links to optimisation and learning landscapes that resonate with my own work on complex systems.
assessment.attribution: Liu and Nagel proposed the jamming phase diagram and drove the theory-experiment programme together; the supplied credit is a natural two-person configuration. Other contributors (for example on isostaticity and critical scaling) are not in the supplied names, so some credit may be left unallocated.
assessment.maturity: Roughly two decades of numerical, theoretical and experimental confirmation; the scaling picture is stable though details such as the relation to glass physics and the exact universality class remain debated. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the physics is judged a single discovery rather than a framework with contested universality
Credit for isostaticity and critical-scaling results by people outside the supplied names
Recollection from memory of the history; I have not independently verified details

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the 2018 observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states opened the field of moire quantum materials and twistronics. The discovery is original, widely reproduced and has produced a very large body of work on strongly correlated and topological phases in a highly tunable platform.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states. This maps onto a fair three-person split; the experimental side also involved Cao and collaborators not in the supplied list, so credit may be contested.
assessment.maturity: Eight years of independent replication across many groups and materials; the core observations are robust, while the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated. Timely but the interpretation is not fully settled.
uncertainties: Unresolved mechanism of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene
Credit for early experimental co-authors outside the supplied names
Possible prematurity relative to interpretive stability

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Intermittency and multifractal scaling are central to the modern understanding of fully developed turbulence: deviations from Kolmogorov 1941 scaling, anomalous exponents and the multifractal formalism. Foundational for a problem of enormous practical importance, from clouds to engineering flows. My own work on particles in turbulence makes me aware both of its importance and of how incomplete a first-principles theory remains.
assessment.attribution: Frisch (multifractal and phenomenological theory, with Parisi) and Sreenivasan (experimental scaling, universality, high-Reynolds-number measurements) are strong representatives, but the field's credit is diffuse (Kolmogorov, Parisi, Benzi, Procaccia, Kraichnan and others). A one-to-three prize is difficult and inevitably leaves out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Decades of experimental and numerical confirmation of anomalous scaling; however the theory is phenomenological and there is no derivation from the Navier-Stokes equations, so the 'discovery' is a robust characterisation rather than a closed solution.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution (Parisi, Kolmogorov lineage, Kraichnan and others)
Lack of a first-principles theory
I work in an adjacent area and should be cautious about my own bias in this field

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, transformed time-keeping and enable searches for variation of constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter tests. Clear, concrete and impactful.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye's group (with JILA collaborators) pushed it to the extreme; the two-name configuration is natural. Other clock groups (for example Lemke, Hinkley, Ludlow, Bloom and others) are not in the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Independent clocks around the world now reach comparable performance and the technology is mature; frequency-comb recognition (2005) and trapped-ion clocks overlap in the chain of credit.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prize-recognised optical frequency-comb and ion-clock work
Possible redefinition of the SI second has not yet occurred, so full impact is pending

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise clean, tunable many-body Hamiltonians (superfluid-Mott transition, fermionic Hubbard physics) and have made quantum simulation a mainstream tool for strongly correlated matter. Important and original, and relevant to the statistical physics of interacting systems.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and Cirac) supplied the theory proposal; Bloch and Greiner performed the Mott transition experiment, with Esslinger and others covering fermionic systems. Five credited names exceed the three-laureate limit, so exclusions are painful. Names such as Dieter Jaksch do not appear in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of confirmation across many laboratories; quantum-gas microscopes and Hubbard-model simulations are mature. Some debate persists about how much has been learned beyond what numerics can reach.
uncertainties: Five credited names versus a three-person limit
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the prior atom-cooling prizes
Whether simulation has so far answered open questions in condensed matter

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, followed by identification of a blazar and the Galactic plane as sources, established neutrino astronomy using a cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice. A major experimental accomplishment with clear lasting scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Halzen led the IceCube concept and realisation; Spiering was a long-term leader of the collaboration and of the predecessor AMANDA/Baikal effort. Credit for a collaboration of hundreds is intrinsically shared, and others such as John Learned, who proposed the underlying detection idea, could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The 2013 discovery has been confirmed with extended datasets and multi-messenger source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068); the field is young so sources remain only partly identified.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit and role of leadership versus design pioneers
Limited number of firmly identified sources

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, theoretically predicted by Kane and Mele and observed in HgTe quantum wells by Molenkamp's group, introduced a new classification of band insulators and launched topological quantum matter. Deep and lasting influence, although it extends the topological classification already recognised by the 2016 prize.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction; Molenkamp led the first experimental realisation (with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's HgTe proposal as an important intermediate step not in the supplied list). A three-person configuration is plausible though Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not available to the committee here.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced extensively in 2D and 3D materials, with robust experiments; applications remain largely prospective, and the novelty relative to the 2016 prize could be argued.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases
Omitted credit for the HgTe prediction

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought cavity QED to superconducting circuits, enabling strong coupling, dispersive readout and the transmon-based architecture that underpins today's superconducting quantum processors. Original and highly consequential.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf (with Wallraff, Huard and Majer) formulated and demonstrated the architecture; the supplied trio is plausible, but credit shared with Wallraff and the 2025 laureates' circuit work should be weighed carefully.
assessment.maturity: The platform is well confirmed and widely adopted, but quantum computing applications are still evolving, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits may reduce the near-term appetite for a closely related award.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits
Credit for Wallraff and other early experimentalists
Whether technological payoff is mature enough
